alt: AdaGrad: the problem (NAG uses one fixed learning rate for all weights), the new concept (each weight gets its own learning rate: frequently updated weights get a smaller rate, rarely updated weights a larger rate) and how it works: calculate the gradient, keep track of past gradients, adjust the learning rate automatically.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: AdaGrad formulas: accumulate gradients G t equals G t minus 1 plus g t squared (element-wise), and the weight update W new equals W old minus eta divided by the square root of G t plus epsilon, times g t. Symbols: eta initial learning rate, g t current gradient, G t sum of past squared gradients, epsilon small value (usually 1e-8).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Advantages of AdaGrad (adjusts the learning rate automatically, no manual tuning, works well with sparse data) and disadvantages (the learning rate continuously decreases, training becomes slower over time, may stop learning before the best solution), with a curve of the learning rate falling toward zero over epochs.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Adam: the problem (momentum remembers the previous direction and RMSProp adjusts the learning rate, but each solves only one problem), the new concept (Adam combines Momentum and RMSProp, fast, stable and efficient training) and how it works in five steps.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Training flow of Adam: mini-batch, forward propagation, loss, backpropagation, gradient g t, momentum (first moment m t), adaptive learning rate (second moment v t), bias correction of m-hat and v-hat, update weights, then back to the next mini-batch.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Adam formulas: first moment m t equals beta 1 m t minus 1 plus (1 minus beta 1) g t, second moment v t equals beta 2 v t minus 1 plus (1 minus beta 2) g t squared, bias correction m-hat and v-hat, and the weight update W new equals W old minus eta m-hat divided by (square root of v-hat plus epsilon). beta 1 is usually 0.9 and beta 2 usually 0.999.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Comparison table of batch gradient descent and SGD: data used (entire dataset or one sample), updates per epoch (one or many), speed (slow or fast), updates (stable or noisy), memory usage (high or low), convergence (smooth or noisy but faster) and best for (small datasets or large datasets and online learning).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Local minimum: the lowest point in a small region of the cost curve, though another point has an even lower loss. A fruit table of losses 20, 8, 12, 2 shows the local minimum at 8 and the global minimum at 2, and gradient descent may stop at loss 8. It happens because complex networks have many valleys.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Loss curve comparison: batch gradient descent takes smooth steps toward the minimum, SGD takes a zig-zag noisy path because the weights are updated after every sample.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Batch size: the number of samples in one mini-batch (common sizes 16, 32, 64, 128). A dataset of 100 fruits with batch size 20 gives 5 mini-batches, so the weights are updated 5 times in one epoch. A second example of 8 fruits with batch size 2 gives 4 batches.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Table comparing batch GD, SGD and mini-batch GD on uses (entire dataset, one sample, small batch), speed, learning path, stability and memory requirement.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Mini-batch gradient descent: what is the problem (SGD updates after every sample, making the path zig-zag), why SGD cannot solve it, the new concept (divide the dataset into small groups called mini-batches and update after each batch) and how it solves the problem in five steps, giving faster learning than batch GD and smoother learning than SGD.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Quick comparison table of global minimum, local minimum and saddle point on lowest loss overall, lowest nearby, best solution, gradient equal to 0, training stops and good for the model.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Momentum gradient descent: it improves gradient descent by remembering the previous weight update, so it also uses the previous direction. A vector picture shows the current gradient and the previous update combining into the new update.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Momentum formulas: velocity update V t equals beta V t minus 1 minus eta times dL/dW and weight update W new equals W old plus V t. V is velocity (momentum), beta the momentum coefficient (usually 0.9), eta the learning rate, L the loss and W the weight.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Loss curve with two paths: mini-batch GD takes a red zig-zag path and momentum GD a smooth curved green path toward the minimum. Key idea: momentum adds speed in the direction of the previous update.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Nesterov accelerated gradient: NAG is an improved version of momentum GD that first looks ahead using the momentum and then calculates the gradient there, giving a better direction, less overshooting and faster convergence. A line diagram shows current position, look-ahead position and update weights.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Loss curve with two paths: momentum GD overshoots slightly near the minimum, NAG takes a smoother path with fewer overshoots. Notes say NAG uses a look-ahead position, computes the gradient there, and gives faster and more stable learning.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A comparison table of momentum, RMSProp and Adam on what each does (remembers the previous direction, adaptive learning rate, combines both), the learning rate, and the main benefit, each with a small loss graph.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: RMSProp: the problem (AdaGrad keeps adding all past squared gradients so the learning rate keeps decreasing), the new concept (RMSProp adjusts the learning rate using only recent gradients, with a moving average of squared gradients) and how it works in five steps, keeping learning fast and stable.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: RMSProp formulas: moving average S t equals beta S t minus 1 plus (1 minus beta) g t squared, and the weight update W new equals W old minus eta divided by (square root of S t plus epsilon) times g t. S t is the moving average of squared gradients, beta the decay rate (usually 0.9).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Fruit example comparing learning rates: for AdaGrad the learning rate keeps decreasing (0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.005, 0.0005) so learning almost stops, while for RMSProp it stays stable (0.1, 0.08, 0.09, 0.07, 0.08) so learning remains fast and stable.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Stochastic gradient descent: the problem with batch GD (it uses the entire dataset for every update, which is slow for large datasets), the definition (update the weights after processing only one training sample at a time) and how SGD works in six steps: pick one sample, forward propagation, calculate loss, backpropagation, update weights immediately, repeat for the next sample.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How SGD works with an example of five fruits (apple, banana, orange, mango, grapes): each fruit updates the weights once, one epoch finishes after all samples are processed, and in multiple epochs the process starts again from the apple.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Gradient descent: the definition (an optimization algorithm that updates the weights and biases to reduce the loss; its goal is to find the minimum loss by moving the weights in the correct direction), its four steps (calculate the gradient, find the direction where the loss decreases, update the weights, repeat until the loss is very small) and a loss curve with dots moving down to the minimum.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Working of gradient descent: six steps (initialize weights randomly, forward propagation, calculate the loss, backpropagation for gradients, update the weights, repeat until the loss is minimum), the formula W new equals W old minus eta dL/dW with symbols, a working flow, what a gradient is, and the learning rate effect (small is slow, large may skip the minimum, proper is fast and stable).
author: Deep Learning faculty
